intro: Alishan is a mountain forest area in Chiayi County, reached by a narrow-gauge railway built to carry cypress down to the plains, and known for its sunrises, its sea of clouds and the giant red cypresses left standing in the recreation area. Its Sacred Tree is a title rather than a fixed tree. The original fell in the late 1990s, and the cypress carrying the name today was chosen by about 25,000 people in a public vote, on a 600 metre boardwalk near Ciyun Temple.
meta_description: The Sianglin Sacred Tree: Alishan's second-generation sacred cypress, chosen by public vote in 2006, 45 metres tall and 12.3 metres round.
question_meta: The Sianglin Sacred Tree is Alishan's second-generation Sacred Tree, a red cypress 45 metres tall, dated at about 626 years by a 2022 study.
question_answer: The Sianglin Sacred Tree stands on Trail 1, a 600 metre boardwalk near Ciyun Temple inside the Alishan National Forest Recreation Area in Chiayi County. It is a Taiwan red cypress, 45 metres tall and 12.3 metres round by the park's own figures, and it was crowned Alishan's second-generation Sacred Tree on 1 January 2007 after roughly 25,000 people voted for it the year before. Its age is disputed: tourism material has long said about 2,300 years, while a 2022 tree-ring study by National Chiayi University dated the main trunk at about 626.
question_context: The dispute has a straightforward explanation. The 2022 study, commissioned by the Forestry Bureau, found that the tree is a merged tree, several red cypress stems that grew into each other over centuries, so the standing mass is much larger than the age of any single dateable trunk would suggest. Neither figure is a mistake, and the older one is still the one most tourism material carries. Dimensions vary a little by source too: the park's own site gives 45 metres of height and 12.3 metres of girth, an older account 43.5 and 13.1, with a diameter at breast height of about 4.1 metres. The tree it succeeded, a red cypress of around 3,000 years, collapsed in heavy rain and was taken down in the late 1990s, which is why Alishan ran the vote at all. Before the crowning this one was known as the Guangwu Cypress, after a provincial governor's belief that it had germinated during the reign of the Han emperor Guangwu. The same boardwalk passes the Thousand-Year Cypress, the Tree of Three Generations and the Tree Spirit Pagoda.

faq.q: How old is the Sianglin Sacred Tree?
faq.a: Sources disagree and both figures are worth knowing. Tourism material has cited roughly 2,300 years for decades. A 2022 tree-ring study by National Chiayi University dated the main trunk at about 626 years, having found that the tree is several red cypress stems fused into one mass rather than a single trunk.

faq.q: Is this the original Alishan Sacred Tree?
faq.a: No. The original was a different and much older red cypress, which collapsed in heavy rain and was taken down in the late 1990s. The Forestry Bureau then ran a public online vote, about 25,000 people took part, and this tree was crowned Alishan's second-generation Sacred Tree on 1 January 2007.
The park's own figures are 45 metres tall and 12.3 metres round, with a diameter at breast height of about 4.1 metres. An older account gives 43.5 metres and 13.1 metres.

No. Entry to the Alishan National Forest Recreation Area costs around NT$300, less for Taiwan residents and students, and the area is open year round. From the gate it is a short walk along the paved 600 metre Trail 1 boardwalk, past Ciyun Temple.
By the Alishan Forest Railway or the Alishan Route B bus from Chiayi Railway Station, roughly 2.5 to 3 hours. Both put you at Alishan Bus Station, just outside the park's entrance gate.

trees.story:
This tree was elected. Alishan's original Sacred Tree, a red cypress of around 3,000 years, was wrecked by storm damage and taken down in the late 1990s, and the Forestry Bureau put the succession to a public online vote. About 25,000 people took part, this cypress won, and on 1 January 2007 the county magistrate crowned it Alishan's second-generation Sacred Tree. Before that it went by Guangwu Cypress, after a provincial governor's conviction that it had germinated during the reign of the Han emperor Guangwu.

Its age is genuinely in dispute, and both numbers are worth carrying. Tourism material has said roughly 2,300 years for decades, some of it stretching to 3,000. Then a 2022 tree-ring study by National Chiayi University, commissioned by the Forestry Bureau, dated the main trunk at about 626 years and explained the gap: what looks like one enormous stem is a merged tree, several red cypresses that grew into each other over centuries. The bulk is real. The single great age is not established, and the older figure is still the one most of the tourism material carries.

The park's own record gives it 45 metres of height and 12.3 metres of girth; an older account says 43.5 and 13.1. It stands on Trail 1, a 600 metre boardwalk near Ciyun Temple that passes the Thousand-Year Cypress and the Tree of Three Generations on the way, so it is a short walk in and not the only giant on it.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the trunk, 12.3 metres round and visibly several stems fused into one mass. It stands on Trail 1, the boardwalk running between Ciyun Temple and Xianglin Elementary School.
trees.access: Paid entry to Alishan National Forest Recreation Area (around NT$300, less for Taiwan residents/students), open year round; from the park entrance it is a short, easy walk along the paved 600 m Trail 1 boardwalk past Ciyun Temple.
trees.transport: Alishan Forest Railway or bus (Alishan Route B) from Chiayi Railway Station, roughly 2.5 to 3 hours; alight at Alishan Bus Station just outside the park's official entrance gate, then walk in.
